question: to the Commission Nadine Morano (PPE) Subject:

Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union points out that national security is the sole responsibility of Member States. However, the digital transformation, especially the increasing use of AI, has profoundly changed how criminal networks operate – they are now exploiting digital technology to develop ever more sophisticated and international activities. To respond to these developments, the Commission is preparing a set of reforms for Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office. Those reforms include the creation of a ‘European police cloud’, which is meant to improve Europol’s exchange of information, operational cooperation and analysis capabilities, in order to step up the fight against crossborder crime and cybercrime. At the same time, the Commission stresses that the new tools must respect fundamental rights and Member States’ powers as regards national security. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the future European police cloud will enable operational data to be shared between national authorities in a manner that is sufficiently comprehensive and homogeneous, while respecting Member States’ prerogatives under Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union?
Does it intend to define a minimum set of information that must be shared, in order to ensure that this new European infrastructure is operationally effective?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) In its proposal for a new European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) Regulation1, the Commission proposes establishing a Police Shared Data Space to make operational data exchange between national authorities faster and more efficient. It would let Member States open joint operational analysis cases (JOACs)2: secure collaborative environments where Member States, Europol and trusted partners would work simultaneously on the same data3, using Europol’s analytical tools4. To ensure comprehensive and homogeneous exchange, the Commission will adopt implementing acts defining the Police Shared Data Space’s functionalities and the modalities to ensure interoperability5. According to the Commission’s proposal, each Member State may decide whether to open a JOAC6, fully respecting their prerogatives7. Currently Member States are obliged to provide Europol with the information necessary for the Agency to fulfil its tasks8. The Commission’s proposal aims at facilitating compliance with that obligation through mandatory data loaders9, which are automated technical means enabling the systematic, structured uploading of relevant information from national case management systems10. According to the Commission’s proposal, competent authorities of the Member States may refrain from uploading data, including where sharing data would harm national security interests or an ongoing investigation11. The sovereignty of cloud infrastructure and services used in the future to deploy the Police Shared Data Space will be ensured in compliance with the requirements of the Cloud and Artificial Intelligence Development Act12, which puts in place appropriate safeguards to protect highly critical public sector activities and systems deployed in the cloud.
